def: A flat blue-gray birthmark over the lower back or buttocks, common in darker-skinned infants. It results from dermal melanocytes and usually fades in childhood; it can be mistaken for bruising.
A closed-loop RNA without free ends, formed by back-splicing, which makes it resistant to exonucleases. Some circular RNAs sponge microRNAs.
A rodent-borne arenavirus endemic to West Africa that causes hemorrhagic fever. It spreads via Mastomys rat excreta and is treated with ribavirin; sensorineural deafness is a common sequela.
The smallest blood vessels, comprising arterioles, capillaries and venules, where exchange occurs. Diabetes damages it, causing retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.
Tumors of the hypothalamus, such as gliomas and germ cell tumors, causing endocrine dysfunction and visual or appetite changes.
Trauma to the newborn during delivery, such as clavicle fracture, brachial plexus palsy, cephalohematoma or caput succedaneum.
Viruses that need a helper virus to replicate. Hepatitis D virus is the key example, requiring hepatitis B surface antigen.
A family of small, single-stranded DNA viruses, including parvovirus B19, which causes erythema infectiosum and aplastic crisis.
A live oral vaccine of adenovirus types 4 and 7 given to military recruits to prevent respiratory illness.
Separation of the choroid from the sclera by fluid or blood, often after eye surgery or with low eye pressure.
Outward deviation of an eye, a form of divergent strabismus. It occurs in oculomotor palsy and intermittent childhood exotropia.
Inward turning of an eye, a form of convergent strabismus. It occurs in abducens palsy and childhood accommodative esotropia.
A fitted mask filtering 95% of airborne particles above 0.3 micrometers. It is used for airborne precautions such as tuberculosis and measles.
An immune-mediated adverse reaction to a medication, ranging from rash to anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Skin cancers other than melanoma, mainly basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, linked to UV exposure.
Repetitive involuntary leg jerks during sleep, causing disrupted sleep. It is associated with iron deficiency, kidney failure and pregnancy.
A calcium-binding protein marker in neural crest-derived cells. It stains melanoma, Schwann cell tumors and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
The skull bone at the back and base, with the foramen magnum through which the spinal cord passes.
A fibrate that activates PPAR-alpha to lower triglycerides.
Proteins needed to import proteins into peroxisomes. Mutations cause Zellweger syndrome.
Backflow of blood from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle in diastole, producing a diastolic decrescendo murmur (Graham Steell).
Pericarditis with fever and pleuritic chest pain weeks after cardiac surgery, from an autoimmune reaction.
A live attenuated vaccine against measles, usually given as MMR.
An inactivated vaccine against hepatitis A virus, given to children and travelers.
A malignant tumor of fibroblasts, with spindle cells in a herringbone pattern.
Immune protection at mucosal surfaces, driven by secretory IgA and MALT.
A ligand-activated transcription factor that responds to dioxins and induces CYP1A1. It also regulates immune cells.
A plastic (PVC) whose vinyl chloride monomer exposure is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
A serine/threonine kinase in the MAPK pathway downstream of RAS. BRAF V600E mutations occur in melanoma, and vemurafenib targets them.
A receptor tyrosine kinase for platelet-derived growth factor, promoting growth of fibroblasts and smooth muscle. It is mutated in GIST and inhibited by imatinib.
A receptor tyrosine kinase whose fusions (EML4-ALK) drive some lung cancers and anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Crizotinib inhibits it.
A T-cell lymphoma with large pleomorphic cells expressing CD30, often with ALK translocation t(2;5).
A tumor suppressor protein from the CDKN2A locus that inhibits MDM2, stabilizing p53.
The gene encoding p16 and p14ARF, tumor suppressors. Its inactivation occurs in melanoma and pancreatic cancer.
A tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 18q, deleted in colorectal cancer, encoding a netrin receptor.
A receptor tyrosine kinase of the ErbB family, amplified in some breast and gastric cancers. Trastuzumab targets it.
An autosomal dominant PTEN hamartoma syndrome with many hamartomas, macrocephaly and increased risk of breast, thyroid and endometrial cancers.
Neuronal RNA-binding proteins targeted in paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis and sensory neuropathy, usually with small cell lung cancer (anti-Hu).
A tumor suppressor that blocks the G1-S transition by binding E2F. Its loss causes retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma.
The tumor suppressor gene encoding merlin on chromosome 22. Mutations cause neurofibromatosis type 2 with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
A rare aggressive cancer of the adrenal cortex, often secreting cortisol or androgens. It is associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
Different forms of an enzyme catalyzing the same reaction but with distinct structure, such as creatine kinase isoforms.
A cell surface protein expressed on mesothelial cells, overexpressed in mesothelioma and pancreatic cancer.
The total amount of tumor in the body, assessed by size, number of lesions or serum markers.
An agent injected into a vessel to cause inflammation and scarring that closes it, used for varicose veins and esophageal varices.
Receptors that bind neurotransmitters, divided into ligand-gated ion channels and G-protein-coupled receptors.
Excess urinary oxalate, causing calcium oxalate kidney stones. Primary forms are genetic, while enteric forms follow fat malabsorption.
The receptor for IL-1 signaling inflammation and fever. Anakinra blocks it.
Surgery removing prostate tissue through the urethra to treat BPH. Hyponatremia from absorbed irrigation fluid (TURP syndrome) is a risk.
Semen flowing backward into the bladder because of failure of bladder neck closure. It is caused by alpha-blockers, diabetes or prostate surgery.
Ventricular fibrillation from a blunt chest blow during the vulnerable phase of the T wave, as with a baseball.
CD4 T cells in germinal centers that help B cells class switch and mature, via CD40L and IL-21.
Surgical opening in the trachea to create an airway.
Hormones made by the placenta, including hCG, progesterone, estrogens and human placental lactogen.
A retrovirus genus with long incubation, including HIV. Lentiviral vectors are used in gene therapy.
Introducing foreign nucleic acid into eukaryotic cells in a lab.
Targeted modification of DNA, for example with CRISPR-Cas9, zinc fingers or TALENs.
Use of electric pulses to create temporary pores in cell membranes so DNA can enter.
RNA that directs Cas9 to its target DNA. crRNA recognizes the target and tracrRNA helps assemble the complex.
A salt of benzoic acid. Sodium benzoate is used in urea cycle disorders to bind glycine and excrete nitrogen.
A cytokine from Th17 and ILC3 cells that promotes epithelial barrier defense and antimicrobial peptides.
T cells expressing NK markers that recognize lipid antigens on CD1d.
A cytokine from Tfh cells that promotes B cell differentiation and plasma cell formation.
A vaccine of purified antigens rather than whole cells, such as the acellular pertussis vaccine.
A protein regulating iron absorption through hepcidin. C282Y mutations cause hereditary hemochromatosis.
A short-acting antimuscarinic eye drop that dilates the pupil and paralyzes accommodation for eye exams.
A selective beta-1 blocker that also increases nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation.
The space behind the peritoneum containing the kidneys, adrenals, aorta, IVC, pancreas and most of the duodenum.
A structured protocol for initial trauma assessment, following airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure.
Reduced vessel compliance that raises systolic and pulse pressure, from aging or atherosclerosis.
Prostaglandin I2, produced by endothelium, which dilates vessels and inhibits platelets. Analogs treat pulmonary hypertension.
The first branch of the aortic arch, dividing into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
Disease from filarial nematodes such as Wuchereria bancrofti, spread by mosquitoes. It causes lymphatic obstruction and elephantiasis.
Surgical connection of the intestine to the liver hilum to restore bile drainage in biliary atresia.
Hyaline cartilage connecting the ribs to the sternum. Costochondritis involves its inflammation.
Proteins forming the cell's structural network, including actin, intermediate filaments and microtubules.
Structural proteins of myelin such as myelin basic protein, PLP and P0. Mutations or autoantibodies cause demyelinating disease.
A tumor arising from cells surrounding nerves, such as schwannoma or neurofibroma.
Sweating and flushing of the cheek while eating, after parotid surgery or injury, from misdirected parasympathetic regrowth.
Impaired pumping or filling of a ventricle, leading to heart failure.
One of two large veins formed by the jugular and subclavian veins that join into the superior vena cava.
A pancreatic trypsin inhibitor protecting against premature trypsin activation. Mutations cause hereditary pancreatitis.
Release of virus particles from an infected host, enabling transmission.
Membrane-associated GTP-binding proteins with alpha, beta and gamma subunits that relay signals from GPCRs.
A technique using fluorescent-labeled antibodies to detect tissue-bound antigens or immune deposits, such as in pemphigus and lupus.
A dipeptide of beta-alanine and methylhistidine found in muscle.
Surgical creation of an opening in the bladder, as in a suprapubic catheter.
Persistent excessive insulin secretion in infants, causing severe hypoglycemia, often from KATP channel mutations.
Failure of the gonads to develop normally, as in Turner syndrome (streak ovaries) or Swyer syndrome.
A severe childhood epilepsy with multiple seizure types, slow spike-and-wave EEG and intellectual disability.
Drugs that activate serotonin receptors, such as triptans (5-HT1B/1D) for migraine.
The upper jaw bone, forming part of the palate, orbit floor and nasal cavity, and containing the maxillary sinus.
Posterior displacement of the eyeball into the orbit, seen in orbital floor blowout fracture.
A congenital double uterus with two cervices, from failure of Mullerian ducts to fuse.
A bone fracture combined with joint dislocation.
The castor bean plant, whose seeds contain ricin and castor oil.
An oil from castor beans used as a stimulant laxative.
A plant toxin from castor beans that inactivates the 60S ribosome by removing adenine from rRNA, halting protein synthesis.
Raised pressure in the anterior leg compartment after tibial injury, causing pain, foot drop and loss of dorsiflexion.
An enzyme that depletes asparagine, used in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Toxicities include pancreatitis and thrombosis.
A mitochondrial disease of myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy, with maternal inheritance.
syn: myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers

def: A brief screening test for mild cognitive impairment.
A false joint at a fracture site caused by failed bone union (nonunion).
Water-soluble proteins that make up the lens and keep it transparent. Aggregation causes cataracts.
An enzyme activating glycogen phosphorylase through phosphorylation. Deficiency causes a glycogen storage disease.
A cortical region on the medial temporal lobe, adjacent to the hippocampus, involved in memory and scene recognition.
Inability to recognize faces, from lesions of the fusiform gyrus (inferior temporal lobe).
A relaxation technique of tensing and relaxing muscle groups in sequence.
An enzyme that oxidizes glucose to gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, used in glucose test strips.
The protein encoded by HTT. CAG repeat expansion causes Huntington disease.
An enzyme adding acetyl groups to histones, loosening chromatin and activating transcription.
Proteins that support neuron survival and growth, such as nerve growth factor and BDNF.
A Gram-negative bacillus in fresh water causing wound infection and diarrhea, notably after leech therapy.
A genus of aquatic Gram-negative rods that cause wound infections and gastroenteritis.
An antimuscarinic drug used to reduce sweating and bladder spasm.
The upper part of the sternum, joining the clavicles and first ribs and forming the sternal angle with the body.
Transfusion of blood into the fetus via the umbilical vein, used for fetal anemia from Rh alloimmunization.
Use of drugs such as clomiphene or gonadotropins to stimulate ovulation in infertility.
A sensory nerve of the posterolateral leg and foot, used for nerve biopsy.
Disconnection of the cerebral hemispheres by cutting the corpus callosum, studied for hemisphere specialization.
A mitochondrial protein that moves cholesterol into mitochondria, the rate-limiting step of steroid synthesis. Mutations cause lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Drugs causing altered perception, such as LSD and psilocybin, acting on 5-HT2A receptors.
The area beneath the tongue, containing sublingual glands and Wharton ducts. Ludwig angina involves its infection.
The ribosomal subunit that binds mRNA and the initiator tRNA (30S in prokaryotes, 40S in eukaryotes).
Meningitis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common adult bacterial cause.
Neck soft tissue injury from rapid acceleration-deceleration, as in rear-end collisions.
Infestation with lice, causing itching.
Transfer of DNA between bacteria via a sex pilus, requiring the F plasmid.
A skin disease with shiny yellow-brown plaques on the shins, often in diabetes.
Gradual death of tissue, as in necrobiosis lipoidica.
Stones in salivary ducts, usually the submandibular, causing pain with eating.
Episodes of muscle weakness with low potassium, caused by calcium or sodium channel mutations and triggered by carbohydrate meals or rest after exercise.
A cytochrome P450 enzyme activating carcinogens like benzo[a]pyrene, linked to lung cancer risk.
Two layers of phospholipids forming the cell membrane, with hydrophobic tails facing inward.
A uterus tilted backward toward the rectum, a common normal variant.
A cytochrome P450 enzyme metabolizing codeine, tamoxifen and many antidepressants. Genetic variants change drug effects.
Formation of new neurons, mainly in the hippocampus and olfactory bulb in adults.
A smooth brain without folds from defective neuronal migration, causing seizures and intellectual disability.
A fracture of both pedicles of C2 from hyperextension.
A hybrid gene made by joining two genes, as in BCR-ABL.
Drugs that block kinase enzymes involved in cell signaling, such as imatinib.
Symptomatic, contagious infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis with cough, night sweats, weight loss and pulmonary cavitation.
A protocol for managing cardiac arrest and arrhythmias.
A tumor suppressor protein that causes cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage. Mutations are the most common in human cancer.
A rigid tube for viewing the rectum and anus.
Loss of a protein's folded structure while the primary sequence is retained, from heat or pH.
A fracture with the bone broken into several fragments.
A drug that reduces anxiety, such as benzodiazepines, buspirone and SSRIs.
Leakage from a surgical connection between bowel segments, causing peritonitis and sepsis.
A catheter placed in an artery for continuous blood pressure monitoring and blood gas sampling.
Tear in the aortic wall of the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) causing tearing chest pain; it needs emergency surgery.
Radiation therapy using sealed sources placed in or near the tumor.
Urothelial bladder cancer not invading the muscularis propria, treated by TURBT and intravesical BCG.
Endoscopic removal of bladder tumors via the urethra, used for diagnosis and staging.
Radioactive drugs used for imaging or therapy, such as technetium-99m and iodine-131.
Damage to a laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness or loss of voice, as in thyroid surgery.
Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.
A fracture of the proximal ulna with radial head dislocation.
Inflammation of the larynx causing hoarseness, usually from viral infection.
An IV calcium salt used for hyperkalemia cardiac toxicity and calcium channel blocker overdose.
A skull fracture with bone fragments pushed inward, risking brain injury.

term: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
def: Death of bone in the femoral head from interrupted blood supply, from fracture, steroids or sickle cell disease.
Tear of the anterior-inferior glenoid labrum after anterior shoulder dislocation.
Fever caused by a medication reaction, with no infection.
Surgical cutting of the lower esophageal sphincter muscle to treat achalasia.
Inflammation of skin folds from friction and moisture, often with candida.
Severe acute pancreatitis with bleeding into the gland, causing Cullen and Grey Turner signs.
A procedure inflating a balloon in a stenotic valve to open it.
Glucose in urine, seen when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold or in SGLT2 inhibitor use.
